summary:
ASTRA is a Python-based desktop prototype designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. Its central feature is real-time, webcam-based health screening using computer vision to observe facial landmarks, eye movements, blinking, head posture, visual tracking, and basic coordination.

The system combines these observations with symptom reporting and simulated health and environmental readings to identify potential warning signs. It provides transparent risk alerts, emergency assistance workflows, health assessment history, PDF medical reports, and simulated communication with a remote physician. An interactive virtual space companion helps users navigate the application and understand its features. A built-in mission simulator enables testing under different health and spaceflight hazard scenarios without requiring access to actual spacecraft or astronauts.

ASTRA addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut well-being in isolated environments where immediate medical support is limited. It is important because timely observations, organized health information, and clear emergency communication can support better decision-making during missions. The prototype is intended for research and demonstration, not clinical diagnosis or operational medical use.
details:
ASTRA – Astronaut Health & Safety Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ASTRA is a Python-based desktop application designed to assist with astronaut health monitoring during space missions. Its primary feature is webcam-based health screening using computer vision. It processes live camera input to detect facial landmarks, monitor eye movements and blinking, observe head posture, and conduct guided visual tracking and basic coordination tests.

The system combines these camera-based observations with symptom questionnaires and simulated physiological and environmental readings. A rule-based risk assessment engine evaluates the available information and generates Low, Moderate, or Critical alerts with explanations. It also includes emergency assistance workflows, health history, PDF medical report generation, and simulated communication with a remote physician.

An interactive virtual space companion guides users through the application, explains features, and helps navigate health assessments. A built-in mission simulator generates different health and spaceflight hazard scenarios, allowing the application to be tested without access to actual astronauts or spacecraft equipment.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Camera-based screening: Uses an ordinary webcam to perform basic visual and functional observations without requiring specialized monitoring hardware.
  • Early warning support: Highlights potentially concerning observations and readings for further attention.
  • Centralized health information: Organizes assessments, symptoms, alerts, and medical reports in one application.
  • Emergency support: Provides structured emergency workflows and access to approved protocol information.
  • Remote medical communication simulation: Demonstrates how health reports could be organized and communicated to medical personnel.
  • Accessible testing: Simulates different mission conditions without requiring expensive equipment or real spaceflight environments.
  • Offline functionality: Keeps core monitoring and application features available locally.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to demonstrate how accessible computer vision and software-based health monitoring can support astronaut well-being during long-duration space missions. By organizing health observations, identifying potential warning signs, and providing structured reports, ASTRA aims to support informed decision-making when direct medical assistance is limited by distance and communication delays.

The project is an educational and research prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic or treatment system.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

Programming language: Python.

Main technologies and libraries:

  • OpenCV – webcam access and image processing.
  • MediaPipe – facial landmarks, eye tracking, and pose estimation.
  • PySide6 – desktop graphical user interface.
  • SQLite – local database and assessment history.
  • NumPy – numerical processing.
  • ReportLab – PDF medical report generation.
  • Pytest – software testing.
  • FastAPI – simulated medical communication, where required.

Hardware: A standard Windows computer with an integrated webcam. No dedicated GPU or specialized medical sensors are required for the core prototype.

Development environment: Python, Visual Studio Code, and Windows 11.

5. How is the project creative?

ASTRA combines webcam-based computer vision, health assessment, risk alerts, emergency workflows, mission simulation, and an interactive virtual space companion in one application. Instead of depending entirely on expensive specialized equipment, it explores how an ordinary webcam can support basic health observations and functional screening.

The virtual companion makes the interface more interactive and approachable, while the mission simulator allows users to explore different scenarios and observe how the system responds. The combination of these features creates a practical demonstration of astronaut health-monitoring concepts.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The project was designed around the unique challenges of human spaceflight:

  • Space radiation: A significant mission hazard that requires appropriate exposure monitoring.
  • Isolation and confinement: Long periods away from family and normal social environments can affect well-being.
  • Distance from Earth: Communication delays can make immediate medical assistance difficult.
  • Microgravity: Changes in gravity can affect balance, coordination, and physical adaptation.
